## The pool of characters

**A living pool.** Today all 18 characters exist from the start, nobody new appears, and the pool only shrinks (an executed spy is gone for good). In longer games with many roles, the pool needs to live:

- **Arrivals come through doors (decided 21 October 2026).** Nobody appears out of the ground. A new character enters the map through a door, a place where a route from beyond the map comes in: the western sea from Keftiu and Ahhiyawa, landing on Arzawa's coast, at Alashiya, Ugarit and Egypt; the eastern road from Elam's lands beyond Susa; the Gulf from Magan; the Red Sea from Punt, once its sea zone is added ("The Red Sea" under Ideas); and the Nile beyond Nubia. Which places are doors is map data, at least wherever an edge market will sit ("Edge markets"), and each door's share of arrivals follows its traffic: a first guess in item 11a, then the edge markets' trade once they are built. Most arrivals are strangers from beyond the map, who take their names from that land's attested names (Linear B for the Aegeans) and their languages from it ("Who speaks what"), so each door brings its own mix, set as data from the history pass: the eastern road and the Gulf, which traded into Babylonia, bring more men with some Akkadian; the western sea brings Aegeans who mostly speak only their own tongue, the traders among them a little of the port's; the southern doors bring mostly strangers with no court's tongue. Some are locals coming home, an Egyptian back from Punt, a Babylonian merchant back from Elam, an Ugaritan back from Keftiu, with their own court's language and the edge's. From the door a newcomer travels like any character, needing passage and taking real seasons, towards wherever his skills and languages pay best ("Where characters are, and what they speak"), so whoever holds a door sees its newcomers first, as Egypt sees Nubia's; item 18 checks that courts far from every door are not starved. A stranger with no court's language still has the work that needs none: trading, carrying wares, working for himself, leading a band at sea. He learns a language by living somewhere, Luwian at Arzawa or Akkadian at Ugarit, and grows into a servant over the years. That is the Sherden's road: they appear as fighting men in Rib-Hadda's letters from Byblos, and the king of Alashiya complains that men of Lukka seize villages in his land year by year (EA 38).
- **Or they rise from the crowd.** The one door inside the map: a man the world already holds becomes someone wherever men act together without a head, a crowd of loose men, a band whose leader has fallen, mutineers, a broken army, a revolt or a fallen court's refugees ("A head rises where men lack one"). He was there all along, uncounted; now he matters. Idrimi was one, a prince of Aleppo who fled, lived among the Habiru and became king of Alalakh ("Idrimi, the outlaw who became king"). This door opens only where its people are, so in peace nearly every newcomer is a stranger, and in war the land supplies its own desperate men. The two doors answer different things: strangers come when the pool is short ("A baseline, not a limit"), each drawn from the seeded stream by the doors' traffic ("Deterministic"), while a head rises when men need one, whatever the pool's size.
- **Who they are (decided 21 October 2026).** A newcomer is data first, like every character: the engine draws his facts and the narrator writes his persona from them. The facts are his origin and door; why he came, from a mix that fits the door (trade, flight, a feud, soldiering, wanderlust); what he carries; his languages; and, for a man risen from the crowd, how he rose. Names come from the attested names of his land, or, where none survive, from a style the history pass sets, marked as invented. One rule keeps the stories honest: beyond the map a backstory may say anything, since nothing on the map can check it or depends on it, while on the map it says only what happened. "He fled a blood feud on Keftiu" is free; "the king of Ugarit owes him" needs a debt tablet. Origins are weighted by distance, as people travelled then: most come from just beyond the edge, Aegeans, highlanders from beyond Susa, men from beyond Nubia, and few from far away. The rarest is a man from the tin lands, since tin crossed Iran from hand to hand and almost nobody made the whole journey: he speaks nothing anyone knows, and he can tell the kings what they never knew, where tin comes from, which changes nothing they can do, since the map ends where their world ended. The western sea also brings the peoples later called the Sea Peoples. Some are already in the letters: the Sherden, fighting men at Byblos, who come through the western door with a homeland as unknown as it still is; and the Lukka, raiding Alashiya (EA 38), and the land of Danuna, named from Tyre (EA 151), which lie on or near the map, so their men come from the crowd or the nearest door. The rest, the Shekelesh, Teresh, Peleset, Tjeker and Weshesh, are first named 140 to 170 years later, under Merneptah and Ramesses III, but a people is older than its first record, so they come too, rarely, as adventurers and soldiers for hire rather than invaders, under their later names, marked in the data as first recorded later. Their age of invasion belongs to a later scenario, as Ahhiyawa as a player does.
- **Natural losses.** Characters die only of risk, never of old age ("No age in this game"; plague today only kills a unit), so arrivals replace losses rather than inflate the pool.
- **Deterministic.** Arrivals and deaths draw from their own seeded random stream, so existing seeds keep their characters and replays stay exact.

**No age in this game (decided 21 October 2026).** Characters have no age, and nobody dies of old age. A median game lasts about fourteen years and most under thirty, so old age would be a minor cause of death; without it, a character dies only of risk: battle, execution, murder, the road, plague or famine. Personas describe experience, such as a seasoned envoy or a new scribe, never an age or a nearing end, because a model told it is old reasons as if it will die soon. Heirs, and the generations they need, are left to a game that spans them.

**Attested characters (decided 21 October 2026).** Characters are real people of the period wherever the sources allow, such as the envoys Mane and Keliya, and every other name follows its region's attested names, from the people dossier ("Grounded in the sources").

- **The core comes from the sources.** An attested person's traits are set from what the sources tell of him: Mane, the pharaoh's envoy held for years by Tushratta, or a scribe known from his tablets. Each game varies them a little, by a seeded amount within a narrow band (a first guess of about 10 points either way on the 0–100 scale), so the essence holds while no game is the same.
- **The persona carries it.** The narrator writes each attested character's persona from his traits and what the sources say, and it stays short, since characters are played by a smaller model with a small budget per call. It describes who he was and how he tends to act, never what history did with him, so the game can go its own way.
- **Stakes still decide.** Traits shape his strategy, as for everyone ("Stakes, not dispositions"); the sources give his starting character, not a script.
- **Kings and vassal rulers** are seats, not characters, and are grounded the same way: script kings' temperaments by default follow what the letters show of them (the balance pass's historical archetypes). From item 17b kings are persons too, each with traits and a strategy as every character has ("One scoreboard for every person" under Victory).
- **Everyone else** is generated: arrivals, and the ordinary people the pool needs, take names from their region's attested names and are marked as generated in the data.
- **Nubians in Egypt's service (decided 21 October 2026).** Nubia is Egypt's own land, so Egypt's starting characters include Nubians: captains of Nubian troops above all, since Nubian soldiers garrisoned Canaan (the men who broke into Abdi-Heba's house, EA 287) and Rib-Hadda begs again and again for troops of Meluhha, the letters' name for Nubia; and the Egyptianised elite, princes raised in Pharaoh's nursery. Hekanefer, prince of Miam, a child of the royal nursery shown later in the tomb of Huy, Tutankhamun's viceroy of Kush, is a candidate for an attested character if the history pass finds that his dates fit 1346. Many such men bore Egyptian names, which is true to them. They speak Egyptian, at a skill set by background, and a Nubian tongue that no court reads but that lets them talk with Nubians from the crowd and from beyond the Nile door, and bridge for them. More Nubians come from Nubia's own crowd and through that door ("Arrivals come through doors", "A head rises where men lack one").

Built with the first character package (build order item 10), from the dossiers of item 6+.

**Enough people, not enough good ones.** The pool must be large enough to staff what the kings need: their armies, envoys and spies. If people are short now and then, kings must bid against each other, which is a good dynamic; chronic shortage at every court is not. The way to get both: plenty of ordinary people, few excellent ones. A king can nearly always find someone; competition is for talent, such as the able general or the trusted envoy. How many people there are is set by a baseline the pool keeps near, not by demand, and the price of the scarce ones by fees (the entries below).

**A baseline, not a limit (decided 21 October 2026).** The starting world, with all its courts, sets the baseline, and it does not shrink as powers fall: a conqueror has fewer rivals bidding against him, but more provinces to govern and more armies to lead, so the world's demand for people stays roughly the same through a game. One effect to watch, not to fix: the realm's own couriers carry its orders, so a bigger empire needs no more characters for its messages, and late games may have a surplus of characters, which means cheap men and more outlaws, and suits the age. The pool therefore keeps near a baseline set from the world, as a population keeps near what its land can carry ("How many characters" below). Below the baseline, arrivals come more often, through the doors ("Arrivals come through doors" above); above it, more rarely. Nobody is removed to meet the number, so the pool is sometimes short and sometimes in surplus, and both are part of the game. City-states becoming powers (build order item 11+) do raise it ("How many characters").

**How many characters (decided 21 October 2026).** About 60 at the start, as a first guess and a setting of the table, like the end cap (as built since, a baseline of about a hundred besides the court scribes, the real people of 1346 taking the places of invented ones; item 18 sets the size from what play shows: build order item 17+). The count comes from the work under way at once with seven powers and the planned map: envoys (two or three per power, 15–20), spies (one or two per power, 7–14), commanders (one per field army, 12–18), merchants and carriers on the main trade routes (the coast, the Nile, the tin road along the Euphrates, the crossings to Alashiya, the Gulf, and overland from Hatti into Syria; 10–15), band leaders, pirates and outlaws (5–8), and enough free people that hiring stays possible (10–15). That is about 60–90, and fewer in practice, since one character holds several errands ("Errands, not roles"). The characters' own calls follow their wake-ups ("Characters sleep like kings"), so what limits the number lies elsewhere:

- **The kings' view.** Every character a king knows adds to every one of his calls, on the dearest model, so a king sees only the characters he has dealt with or heard of, and his view does not grow with the pool. A human player likewise follows only those he knows, so each court still deals with a cast of known figures.
- **Waves of wake-ups.** A great event wakes everyone it touches as its news arrives; that spike, not the average, is what to watch.

Item 8 measures wake-ups per character and calls per season once characters are agents; item 18 sets the default from them. At item 11+, when some twenty city-states become powers that write letters, the pool is recounted and grows with them; their rulers get no households of their own, since nothing yet gives kin a motive. A power's starting staff follows its size, so a great king starts with more servants than a city-state.

**Where characters are, and what they speak (decided 21 October 2026).** A shortage of characters now slows the game and makes service dearer; it no longer stops it, since couriers, caravans, ships, levies and policing do a kingdom's routine work, and only a voice or judgement needs a character. Where the shortage falls is shaped twice. Characters gather where the money is, at rich courts and on the trade roads. And they serve only where they can be understood: a character trades anywhere, since markets need no language, but carries a letter to a court or serves there only if he speaks its language or the lingua franca, and he learns a language only by living there ("Languages"). So a court with a rare tongue finds fewer servants and pays more for them: Pharaoh wrote to Arzawa in Hittite, not Akkadian (EA 31). Who understands at a court is whoever serves it there: the king, or anyone in his service at court who speaks the language, a scribe, a resident envoy, anyone he pays to stay (decided 29 October 2026, build order item 11f; Haakon: "Dont they only need someone present at court who speaks akkadian? So anyone they pay to stay there can do the job?"). So every court that reads Akkadian starts with an Akkadian-speaking scribe in its service, as the archives show it, the Amarna letters having been read and written by such scribes at Akhetaten and at every court that answered them; he is paid like any servant and may die, leave or be hired away, and a court that finds envoys going unheard hires another. Language is a character's capital, and years spent at a court make him worth more there. Learning has a price: a character may go to a court on his own and live there to learn, but he pays his own living and earns nothing meanwhile, a cost in gold and in what he could have earned. So the better ways in are paid ones: posted there as an envoy or resident by a king, the usual way in; trading in its market, which needs no language, so he earns while he learns; or, unluckily, held there as a captive or a detained envoy, who comes home with the language at least. No rule is needed: living costs and fees already set the price. Kings have the matching move: posting a new envoy abroad is also an investment in a future servant who speaks the language, much as Thutmose III had the sons of Levantine rulers raised at his court and sent home to rule (a precedent only, since the game has no heirs). Two things to measure, in items 11b, 12 and 18: how many seasons each court's letters wait for a carrier who can be understood where they are going, and whether fees rise until service pays again when working for oneself pays better ("Fees clear the market").
